legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Intelligent AI Delegation", Nenad Tomašev, Matija Franklin, Simon Osindero (Google DeepMind). arXiv:2602.11865v1 [cs.AI], 12 Feb 2026. Preprint, conceptual framework paper.

COVERAGE: 159,623 of 159,623 chars extracted (42 of 42 pages). Body is pp.1-28 (through Conclusion). References run pp.28-42 and were skimmed only for origins. There are no appendices. Extraction was clean. I also read the target note 07-autonomy-ladder.md first. Local copy of the extraction: /tmp/tom.txt.

NATURE OF THE PAPER (answers your question): it is a conceptual and position framework with NO experiments, NO datasets, NO benchmarks and NO measured results. It has no results tables. Tables 1-3 are taxonomies, and Figures 1-2 are flowcharts. Nothing in it can be cited as an empirical finding. The only numbers are illustrative: bid and token examples, the example level names L0-L3, and "quality score: 0.87". Cite it as framework or design argument only.

CLAIMS (ranked; all are arguments, "number: none" unless stated)

1. Delegation is more than task decomposition: it requires transfer of authority, responsibility, accountability, role boundaries and trust mechanisms.
 number: none. setup: definition, Sec 2.1; no experiments.
 quote: "a sequence of decisions involving task allocation, that also incorporates transfer of authority, responsibility, accountability, clear specifications regarding roles and boundaries, clarity of intent, and mechanisms for establishing trust between the two (or more) parties."
 where: Abstract and Sec 2.1 (p.2, lines ~89-98).

2. Autonomy is a per-delegation, non-static grant. The paper separates atomic execution from open-ended delegation. The grant is constrained by market cost or by the delegator's trust model.
 number: none. setup: Sec 4.2.
 quote: "We distinguish between atomic execution, where agents adhere to strict specifications for narrowly scoped tasks, and open-ended delegation, where agents are granted the authority to decompose objectives and pursue sub-goals. This level of autonomy should not be static; it may be constrained implicitly by market costs or explicitly by the delegator's trust model."
 where: p.10.

3. Trust sets autonomy and oversight (graduated authority). Higher trust lowers monitoring cost. Low-trust agents get caps and mandatory oversight.
 number: none. setup: Sec 4.6.
 quote: "graduated authority results in low-trust agents facing strict constraints, such as transaction value caps and mandatory oversight, while high-reputation agents operate with minimal intervention."
 also: "Higher trust enables the delegator to incur a lower monitoring and verification cost."
 where: p.16-17.
 Link to the note: this is the framework version of "earn each handoff with a verifier". Reputation is public history, while trust is a private, context-specific threshold. A high-reputation agent can still miss a high-stakes trust threshold.

4. Contract-first decomposition. Delegation is conditional on the outcome being verifiable. If a sub-task is too subjective, costly or complex to verify, decompose it further until units match the available verification (unit tests, formal proofs). This closely mirrors the note's "no rung 2 without a measurable end state".
 number: none. setup: Sec 4.1, 4.8.
 quote: "task delegation is contingent upon the outcome having precise verification. If a sub-task's output is too subjective, costly, or complex to verify (see Verifiability in Section 4.2), the system should recursively decompose it further."
 where: p.9.
 Verifiability is one of 11 task attributes (Sec 2.2). High verifiability allows "trustless" delegation. Low verifiability "require[s] high-trust delegatees or expensive, labor-intensive oversight".

5. Reversibility and criticality decide the response to failure. Reversible failures get automatic re-delegation. Irreversible, high-criticality failures get termination or human escalation.
 number: none. setup: Sec 4.4.
 quote: "Reversible sub-task failures may trigger automatic re-delegation, whereas failures in irreversible, high-criticality tasks must trigger immediate termination or human escalation."
 where: p.13.
 Sec 2.2(i): irreversible tasks "require stricter liability firebreaks and steeper authority gradients".

6. Permissions by stakes: low-stakes tasks get default standing permissions. High-stakes tasks get just-in-time, task-scoped access with mandatory human-in-the-loop approval. Sub-delegation must use privilege attenuation (a strict subset of authorities). Revocation uses algorithmic circuit breakers, and rules are policy-as-code.
 number: none. setup: Sec 4.7.
 quote: "access to sensitive APIs or control systems is instead granted on a just-in-time basis, strictly scoped to the immediate task's duration, and, where appropriate, gated by mandatory human-in-the-loop approval or third-party authorisation."
 quote: "if an agent's reputation score drops suddenly (see Section 4.6) or an anomaly detection system flags suspicious behavior, active tokens should be immediately invalidated across the delegation chain."
 where: p.18. This maps to note 07's rung 3 vs rung 4 credential point.

7. Human oversight needs context-aware "cognitive friction", balanced against alarm fatigue. Too-frequent verification requests make overseers default to heuristic approval.
 number: none. setup: Sec 5.1.
 quote: "If verification requests for delegation sub-steps are sent to human overseers too frequently, overseers may eventually default to heuristic approval, without deeper engagement and appropriate checks."
 quote: "the system should allow seamless execution for for tasks with low criticality or low uncertainty, but dynamically increase cognitive load, by requiring justification or manual intervention when the system encounters higher uncertainty or is faced with unanticipated scenarios."
 where: p.22-23. Relevant to the note's point that approving each tool call pushes humans toward rubber-stamping.

8. Moral crumple zone and zone of indifference. Humans can keep nominal authority without real control and absorb liability. The AI delegatee's "zone of indifference" is defined by safety filters and system instructions. In chains A→B→C a broad zone lets intent mismatches propagate, and agents become "unthinking routers". The remedy is "dynamic cognitive friction".
 number: none. setup: Sec 2.3, 5.1.
 quote: "it is important to avoid instantiating a moral crumple zone (Elish, 2019), in which human experts lack meaningful control over outcomes, yet are introduced in delegation chains merely to absorb liability."
 where: p.5 and p.22.

9. Liability firebreaks for long chains. Pre-defined stop-gaps where an agent either assumes full non-transitive liability downstream, or halts and requests an updated transfer of authority from the human. Responsibility is transitive up the chain, and "cannot absolve themselves of accountability by blaming subcontractors".
 number: none. setup: Sec 5.2, 4.8.
 quote: "1. Assume full, non-transitive liability for all downstream actions... 2. Halt execution and request an updated transfer of authority from the human principal."
 where: p.23.

10. Paradox of automation and de-skilling. Automating routine work removes the situational awareness humans need for edge cases. The paper proposes deliberately delegating some tasks to humans, and requiring rationales or pre-mortems.
 number: none. setup: Sec 5.6 (cites Bainbridge 1983).
 quote: "This leads to a fragile setup where humans retain accountability for outcomes but lose the hands-on experience required to resolve critical failures."
 where: p.24. Also warns of eroding the apprenticeship pipeline.

11. Span of control. How many agents one human can reliably oversee without fatigue, at an acceptably low error rate, is flagged as an open, goal- and domain-dependent question. No figure is given.
 quote: "it is crucial to establish how many AI agents a human expert can reliably oversee without excessive fatigue, and with an acceptably low error rate."
 where: p.4. Centralised orchestrators are bounded by the same limit (Sec 4.4).

12. Contingency theory: oversight level should be dynamically matched to the task, not fixed. Stable environments suit rigid verification. High-uncertainty ones suit ad-hoc escalation instead of pre-defined checkpoints.
 quote: "high-uncertainty scenarios require adaptive coordination where human intervention occurs via ad-hoc escalation rather than pre-defined checkpoints."
 where: p.6. Useful counterweight to the note's fixed-ladder framing.

13. Monitoring taxonomy (Table 2), five axes: target (outcome vs process), observability (direct vs indirect), transparency (black vs white box), privacy (full vs cryptographic), topology (direct vs transitive). It adds "transitive accountability via attestation": B monitors C and signs a report, and A monitors B's ability to monitor C. Caveat: CoT may not faithfully reflect internal state (Turpin et al., 2023). Proposed monitoring-stream levels are L0_IS_OPERATIONAL, L1_HIGH_LEVEL_PLAN_UPDATES, L2_COT_TRACE and L3_FULL_STATE (p.27).
 where: p.14-16, 27.

14. Delegation overhead and a complexity floor: low-criticality, high-certainty, short tasks should bypass delegation protocols.
 quote: "a complexity floor is established, below which tasks characterised by low criticality, high certainty, and short duration may bypass intelligent delegation protocols in favour of direct execution."
 where: p.12.

15. Adaptive coordination triggers (Fig 2). External triggers: spec change, cancellation, resource change, higher-priority task, security-flagged malicious action. Internal triggers: degraded performance, budget overrun, failed verification of an artifact, unresponsive delegatee. It adds stability measures against oscillation: cooldowns, damped reputation updates, fees on re-delegation. p.12-14.

16. Reliability premium and safety floors. High-assurance verification adds latency and cost. The authors want tiered service levels, a "minimum viable reliability" baseline for all users, and mandatory verification for classes like financial transactions. p.23.

17. Protocol gaps: MCP gives binary access with no semantic attenuation, and no reputation or liability. A2A accepts "completed" with no verification, and has no proof header. AP2 has no conditional settlement. UCP is commerce-specific. p.25-26. Proposed Delegation Capability Tokens (Macaroons/Biscuits) allow read-only, folder-scoped sharing and restriction chaining (p.27).

LIMITS
- No experiments or measurements. Every recommendation is argued, not tested.
- Much of the framework depends on blockchain, smart-contract escrow, zk-SNARKs, TEEs and decentralised markets. The authors concede it is "illustrative", "neither comprehensive, nor meant as a definitive proposal" (p.27). Little of this is deployed today.
- The protocol discussion is selected "based on their popularity" and may have dated (MCP, A2A, AP2, UCP, as of early 2026).
- No autonomy-level scale like the note's four rungs. The paper has no named ladder. Its autonomy axes are: task-level atomic vs open-ended, granularity, monitoring (continuous, periodic or event-triggered), and trust-graduated authority. Do not attribute a rung scheme to it.
- It says nothing on cron triggers, /goal or /loop. The closest overlap is the verifier-before-handoff idea (claim 4) and credential scoping (claim 6).
- It concedes verification is fallible: subjective tasks "can lead to disagreements even when precise rubrics are used" (p.19). It proposes optimistic dispute with bonds and arbitration panels.
- The cognitive-friction vs alarm-fatigue balance is stated as a design goal with no tested thresholds.
- The Sec 2.3 footnote cites deceptive-alignment work (Greenblatt et al. 2024; Hubinger et al. 2024; Needham et al. 2025; van der Weij et al. 2025) as evidence that models can tailor behaviour when evaluated. It is context only.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
Castelfranchi & Falcone 1998 (theory of delegation); Falcone & Castelfranchi 2002 (degrees of autonomy); Ouchi & Dowling 1974 (span of control); Alkov et al. 1992 (authority gradient, aviation); Bainbridge 1983 (Ironies of automation); Elish 2019 (moral crumple zone); Parasuraman et al. 1993 (over-reliance); Williamson 1979/1989 (transaction cost economics); contingency theory (Donaldson 2001); principal-agent literature; Hardy 1988 (confused deputy); Vezhnevets et al. 2017 (FeUdal Networks); Smith 1980 (Contract Net Protocol); Kasirzadeh & Gabriel 2025 (autonomy characterisation); Birgisson et al. 2014 (Macaroons); Lightman et al. 2023 (process-level monitoring); Bowman et al. 2022 (scalable oversight); Teutsch & Reitwießner (TrueBit, verification games); Tomasev et al. 2025 (virtual agent economies); Shao et al. 2025 (cited only in the intro as enterprise work; the note already cites arXiv:2506.06576 separately).

CODE (verbatim, p.27; illustrative protocol extension)
"verification_policy": {"mode": "strict", "artifacts": [{"type": "unit_test_log", "validator": "mcp://test-runner-agent", "signature_required": true}, {"type": "zk_snark_trace", "circuit_hash": "0xabc123...", "proof_protocol": "groth16"}], "escrow_trigger": true}
Also the bid_object (agent_id "did:web:fast-coder.ai", estimated_cost "5.00 USDC", estimated_duration "300s", privacy_guarantee "tee_enclave_sgx", reputation_bond "0.50 USDC"). These are illustrative values only.
Capability-token example, quote: "This token can access the designated Google Drive MCP server, BUT ONLY for folder Project_X AND ONLY for READ operations." (p.27)

FIGURES (the captions command printed nothing, so these come from the text extraction; the images need a render to inspect)
- Fig 1, p.11: "A flowchart of Task Decomposition and Task Assignment." Shows the decompose, verify-granularity, match, contract path. It is the best single picture of contract-first decomposition. I did not view the image.
- Fig 2, p.13: "The adaptive coordination cycle. Different types of environmental triggers may prompt a dynamic re-evaluation of the delegation setup, necessitating runtime changes." This is the monitor, diagnose, respond, escalate cycle, the strongest candidate for the note. Reversibility selects the response.
- Table 1, p.9: five pillars mapped to protocols (§4.1-4.9).
- Table 2, p.15: monitoring taxonomy, lightweight vs intensive.
- Table 3, p.17: reputation models (ledger, web of trust, behavioural).
Fig 2 and Table 2 are the most useful for note 07. All figures are the authors' own, so they would need attribution and a licence check (arXiv).

PROBLEMS
- Extraction drops many spaces in some lines (e.g. "frameworkisapplicabletobothhumanandAIdelegators"). Meaning is intact.
- Fig 1 and Fig 2 content is graphical and did not extract beyond captions, and I did not view the images.
- Sec 2.2 text says "see Verifiability in Section 4.2" but verifiability is defined in 2.2(h). This is a cross-reference slip in the paper.
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF.
- The /tmp/tom.txt file is scratch and not part of the repo.

SUGGESTED USE FOR NOTE 07 (caller decides): this is a sharpens/extends source, not an evidence source. Fit with the note: claims 3, 4 and 6 back "earn each handoff with a verifier" and the rung-4 credential point. Claims 7 and 8 back "unattended, not governed" and the rubber-stamp risk. Claim 10 backs "plan the way back down" (de-skilling) and claim 12 qualifies a fixed ladder. Label every one as an argument, not a measured result.
